analysis.one_liner: Limits commercials in children's TV and forces broadcasters to air and identify educational kids' programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee after one hearing in July 1989 and expired when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap commercials in children's television at 9.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes on weekdays, require stations to publicly identify educational programs for children, and make the FCC weigh a station's children's programming when deciding whether to renew its broadcast license. It was introduced by Senator Tim Wirth in June 1989 and died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families gain: less commercial pressure during children's programming, clearer public notice of which shows are actually educational, and a license-renewal process that takes a station's service to children into account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families watching broadcast TV

how_it_helps.text: Caps commercial matter in children's programming at 9.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays starting January 1, 1990.

Requires stations to announce in advance — and again right before each broadcast — which programs are specifically designed to serve the educational and informational needs of preschool and school-aged children, so parents can identify them.

Directs the FCC to consider a station's compliance with the ad limits and its children's educational programming when reviewing a broadcast license renewal, restoring enforcement power to a process the bill's findings describe as vague and unenforceable.

analysis.who_pays: Broadcast television stations and advertisers lose: less commercial time to sell during children's programming, and children's programming becomes a factor that can cost them their FCC license at renewal time.

drawbacks.text: Cutting commercial minutes in children's programming reduces the advertising revenue that pays for children's shows, which broadcasters would argue could shrink the amount of children's programming stations choose to air.

The cap applies to a very broad definition of 'commercial matter' — anything broadcast for money or barter, even if not purely commercial — and puts the burden on stations to prove barter deals are fair, which gives the FCC wide power over program content aimed at children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to children is real and specific: fewer ads aimed at them and honest labeling of educational shows. The main cost falls on broadcasters and advertisers, not on families, though broadcasters' warning that lower ad revenue means less children's programming deserves to be taken seriously. The bill's own enforcement hook — counting children's service at license renewal — is what gives it teeth, and it is also the part incumbents would resist most.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1989, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing in July, and died there when the Congress ended in January 1991 without a committee vote or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Wirth of Colorado introduced the Children's Television Education Act of 1989 on June 21, 1989, joined by two Senate Democrats as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on June 21, 1989.
The Communications Subcommittee held hearings on July 12, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-221; that was the bill's last action.
No committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action occurred before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadcasters and advertisers kept unrestricted commercial time in children's programming, since the ad caps, notice requirements, and license-renewal scrutiny never became law.

for.name: Sen. Tim Wirth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set out its findings that broadcasters were failing children and the FCC had made its children's obligations vague and unenforceable.

for.name: Sens. Howard Metzenbaum and Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in June 1989, held one subcommittee hearing in July, and never reported it out for a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Association of Broadcasters
against.what_they_did: The broadcasting industry consistently opposed new restrictions on advertising time in children's programming during this era.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Senate Democrats were attached to the bill — Wirth, Metzenbaum, and Lautenberg — and no Senate Republicans signed on; the committee that shelved it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill cuts the commercial minutes stations can sell in children's programming and makes their service to children a condition of keeping their FCC licenses. Stations profit from selling the audience's time to advertisers, so the caps directly cut that revenue.

industries.industry: Children's TV advertisers (toys, cereal, snack makers)
industries.note: Fewer commercial minutes per hour means less access to a highly valuable child audience, which is why the weekend cap is set lower than the weekday cap. The broad definition of 'commercial matter' also covers paid and bartered program content.
